0.0.n: 皆さん politely addresses the whole audience; さん adds respect.

0.1.n: This standard daytime greeting ends with は, pronounced わ.

0.3.n: Combines with 教師 to specify which language she teaches.

0.4.n: 教師 is a neutral job title, often used when describing your own profession.

0.5.n: の links the job title to the name, identifying Mirai as a Japanese teacher.

0.6.n: 未来 is the speaker’s name here, not the ordinary word for future.

0.7.n: です politely completes the introduction; the speaker leaves out I.

1.0.n: 今日 sets the time for the suggested practice.

1.1.n: は marks 今日 as the topic: what they will do today.

1.2.n: 一緒 pairs with に to describe doing the practice with someone else.

1.3.n: に turns 一緒 into a phrase describing how they will practice.

1.4.n: 旅行 names the activity in which the Japanese will be useful.

1.5.n: で marks travel as the situation where the Japanese is useful.

1.6.n: 役立つ is in its plain form and describes 日本語 later in the sentence.

1.8.n: ホテル is a borrowed word written in katakana; Japanese does not distinguish singular and plural here.

1.9.n: で marks the hotel as the place where the Japanese is used.

1.10.n: 使う comes before 日本語 to describe it: Japanese that you use at hotels.

1.11.n: Here 日本語 refers to the language and expressions they will practice.

1.12.n: を identifies 日本語 as the thing receiving the action of practicing.

1.13.n: 練習する becomes 練習しましょう, a polite invitation to do the activity together.

0.lit: Everyone, hello. Japanese-language teacher Mirai am.
0.tip: Job title + の + name is a natural way to introduce yourself with your profession.

1.lit: Today, together, useful during travel, used at hotels, Japanese let’s practice.
1.tip: Both 役立つ and ホテルで使う describe 日本語, with these descriptions placed before the noun.
